geo.label: risk-off into payrolls
parts: Macro Stance

Risk assets are in a rout into a data gap. The S&P 500 suffered its fifth loss in six days, led by AMD’s 17.3% drop [[n8096]]. Private payrolls rose by only 22,000 in January, well short of expectations, according to ADP [[n7240]], and the official January jobs report has been pushed to February 11 after the shutdown delay [[n7230]]. Activity is not the problem: the ISM services index for January came in at 53.8% [[n7223]], and Reuters reports the sector steady, with AI data-centre supply constraints feared [[n7225]]. The Fed is the policy wildcard. Governor Cook says it is time to wait and see on rates [[n8026]], and Senator Scott is facing a block on the Fed chair nominee [[n8032]]. We are Bearish on equities into the payrolls print, with the bond market providing the only offset.
Rates & Curve

The 2-year Treasury yield closed the prior session at 3.57% and the 10-year at 4.29%, with the 3-month bill at 3.69%, the 5-year at 3.83% and the 30-year at 4.91% (US Treasury, prior close 2026-02-04). The 10Y−2Y spread is 72 bps and the 10Y−3M spread is 60 bps. Over 20 observations the 2-year rose 10 bps and the 10-year rose 11 bps, so the spread widened by 1 bp; over five observations the 2-year rose 1 bp and the 10-year rose 3 bps. The card reads the curve as “moderately steep, approaching the long-run average” and the move as “bear steepening (both up, 10Y up more)”, which matches this session’s figures. Investors are ramping up bets on a steeper curve under a Warsh-led Fed [[n8022]]. The S&P 500 closed at 6,882.72, down 0.51% in the prior session and 0.89% over 20 sessions, while the VIX closed at 18.64, up 14.0% over five sessions and 26.4% over 20 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-04). The Nasdaq 100 fell 1.77% in the prior session.
New / Most Important

The most important story is the software and services rout. Analysts put a loss of nearly $1 trillion across software and services stocks as investors debate whether AI is an existential threat to the business model [[n8061]]. Anthropic’s new AI tools deepened the selloff in data analytics and software stocks [[n8060]], and Nvidia’s chief executive called the software selloff the most illogical thing in the world [[n5972]]. Against that, the Fed is in a governance argument: Treasury Secretary Bessent says the Fed lacks accountability and has lost public trust [[n8024]], while the Fed keeps bank capital buffers steady until 2027 [[n8021]]. The government shutdown has ended, and the funding bill is signed [[n8129]].
Playbook ✓

Bearish into the February 11 payrolls print [[n7230]]: reduce software and AI-disruption exposure and keep a hedge on the S&P 500 through software-heavy names rather than through broad index puts. Keep duration near neutral until the jobs data settles the curve question; the 10-year at 4.29% is the level to watch, and a close above it with the spread widening would argue for trimming duration. Turn Bullish on the broad market if the VIX, now at 18.64, falls back below its 20-session starting level and the Nasdaq 100 stops falling over five sessions. Turn more Bearish if the jobs report confirms the ADP shortfall and the Warsh confirmation stalls.

geo.label: disinflation / record STOXX
parts: Macro Stance

The euro area is disinflating while the STOXX Europe 600 holds near record levels. Euro-zone inflation fell to the lowest rate in more than a year [[n2681]], and the FT puts January inflation at 1.7% [[n2682]]. Reuters describes the euro-zone soft patch as beginning [[n2680]]. The ECB has little reason to move in either direction yet, but a fall in inflation makes a cut later in the year more credible than it was. We are Bullish on European equities for the disinflation story, with the ECB as a source of optionality rather than a current catalyst.
Credit & Inflation

Euro-area inflation is the reason the bond market is calm. The January reading is the lowest in more than a year [[n2681]], which eases the pressure on the ECB, and the euro-zone economy is described as having a soft patch rather than a recession [[n2680]]. The credit side is less comforting: euro-zone banks are tightening access to business credit [[n2626]], and the ECB survey showed an unexpected tightening in bank lending [[n2624]]. EUR/USD closed at 1.1816 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-04), up 1.09% over 20 sessions and down 1.68% over five. The Bank of England held rates, and sterling slipped as the dollar hit a two-week high [[n2724]].
New / Most Important

The European stock market set a record even as technology and health care dragged. Reuters reports the European stocks closing at a record high [[n2701]], and European chemical stocks surged on emission-rule optimism [[n2703]]. The AI-disruption trade is hitting European software too: global software stocks were hit by the Anthropic wake-up call [[n2705]], and the UK economy gathered pace at the start of 2026 [[n2693]] even as services job cuts continued as companies automate [[n2719]]. Germany’s chancellor is looking for new partners in Saudi Arabia and the Gulf [[n2694]].
Playbook ✓

Bullish: own European cyclicals and banks against US software and AI-platform exposure, and keep the DAX as the laggard that could catch up. The STOXX 600 closed at 618.12 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-04), up 2.17% over 20 sessions, while the DAX fell 2.07% over the same period and the FTSE 100 rose 3.52%. The call turns Bearish if the euro strengthens quickly against the dollar on a hawkish ECB repricing, or if the software selloff spreads to the European banks through their private-credit books.

geo.label: tax tightening / onshore calm
parts: Macro Stance

China is tightening at the margin while the official data stay soft. Beijing is raising taxes on select sectors [[n1051]], and provinces have set lower growth targets for 2026 [[n1052]]. The official January manufacturing PMI was 49.3 [[n0783]], and a private survey shows factory activity expanding at the fastest pace since October [[n0855]]. Services picked up, with hiring at a six-month high [[n0998]]. We stay Mixed: the tax and target decisions argue against a policy surge, while the services data and onshore stability argue against a hard slowdown.
PMIs & Activity

The factory data disagree. The official PMI reading of 49.3 [[n0783]] is a contraction, while a private survey shows factory activity expanding [[n0855]] and expansion accelerating in January [[n0857]]. The feed also carries the Bloomberg headline that China’s factory activity unexpectedly slid into contraction [[n0781]], which is the official-side reading. Services activity picked up and hiring hit a six-month high in January [[n0998]], which is the strongest of the three series. We weight the services and hiring series above the factory surveys because they are less exposed to export swings.
Credit Impulse

The feed has no fresh January credit print. The clearest policy signal is the PBOC’s key bank loan rate, which fell to a record low [[n0880]], a cut that supports borrowing rather than proving it. Local-government land-sales income fell double digits for a fourth straight year in 2025 [[n0918]], which removes a funding source for local credit. Beijing’s $29 billion special-bond plan for insurers [[n0773]] is the recapitalisation channel, not a stimulus. The confirming signal is a January new-loan print that stops shrinking; until then the credit impulse is not a reason to add China cyclicals.
Property

Property has not turned. The sector started 2026 with a bleak sales outlook as sales declines accelerated [[n7164]], and developers say the hopeful signs are not real [[n7167]]. Shanghai is buying small older flats to revive its housing market [[n1007]], China Vanke warned of an $11.8 billion loss for 2025 [[n0828]], and Hang Lung says sentiment is not fully back [[n0868]]. Measures to shore up the indebted sector were announced [[n0841]], but the feed gives no sign that they have changed the sales trend.
Fiscal, Policy & Trade

Policy is pro-consumption in words and cautious in money. A top official vowed to boost consumption to overhaul the economy [[n0990]], and China logged its first fiscal revenue drop since 2020 on the property slump [[n0785]]. It undershot its 2025 spending goal in a sign of caution on debt [[n0776]]. On trade, the US proposed a critical-minerals trade bloc aimed at countering China [[n1065]], and South Korea is seeking critical-minerals ties with China after joining it [[n1073]]. Beijing is also piloting digital-yuan interest payments [[n1038]] and LNG futures [[n1042]].
Markets & Flows

The Shanghai Composite closed at 4,102.20 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-04), up 0.85% in the prior session and down 1.18% over five sessions, and up 0.40% over 20. The Hang Seng closed at 26,847.32, up 1.47% over 20 sessions. The China A-share ETF ASHR closed at 33.48, down 1.65% over 20 sessions; the offshore internet ETF KWEB at 33.42, down 8.04%, and KWEB fell 2.91% in the prior session; the large-cap ETF FXI at 38.27, down 4.11%; and USD/CNY at 6.9377, down 0.65% over 20 sessions. Onshore retail is still in the market: 4.9 million new accounts were opened in January [[n1010]], and China’s gold trading hub is on edge [[n0991]].
New / Most Important

The headlines disagree on Hong Kong. One says the tax worries abated and solar stocks rallied on Musk-linked plans [[n1087]]; another says Hong Kong-listed tech stocks entered a bear market as tax and AI fears took hold [[n1088]]. We give no direction on that conflict. What is clear is that the AI-revenue fear is spreading to the Chinese tech complex: a Fortune headline says tech stocks went into free fall as it dawned on traders that AI could cut revenues across the board [[n1086]]. Chinese solar shares jumped on reports that SpaceX and Tesla staff visited suppliers [[n1090]].
Playbook ✓

Stay Mixed: favour onshore policy beneficiaries and the solar and grid supply chain over offshore internet names, and keep the yuan on a managed path. Watch the January credit print: a rise in new loans would confirm the policy story; a second weak print would argue for holding offshore China exposure at a lower weight. ⚠ Divergence: the solar and supplier rally in onshore names [[n1090]] is running against an offshore internet ETF that is down 8.04% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-04).

geo.label: bond rout / yen under pressure
parts: Macro Stance

Japan’s bond market is the stress point before the election. Reuters reports that the BOJ will not come to the rescue of a bond rout driven by PM Takaichi’s policies [[n3556]], and the Japan Times warns that the bond market has a lesson for America [[n3563]]. Takaichi’s own reflationist aide has called for fiscal discipline [[n3561]], a sign that the government is split. The Morningstar analysis sees a risk of future fiscal constraint with limited impact on equities [[n3554]]. We are Bearish on Japanese duration and the yen until the vote clarifies the fiscal plan.
Activity & Currency

USD/JPY closed at 155.7990 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-04), up 2.19% over five sessions and down 0.56% over 20. The yen is under pressure ahead of the election [[n8112]], and the yen’s weakness was the subject of a finance-ministry defence of the PM’s remarks [[n3496]]. Hedge funds revived yen-weakness trades ahead of the vote [[n3531]]. Corporate results are mixed: Sony posted a 22% jump in profits despite the memory crunch [[n3564]], Toyota is expected to post a third straight quarterly profit drop [[n3562]], and MUFG’s profit rose on the BOJ’s rate increases [[n3558]]. The Nikkei 225 closed at 54,293.36, down 0.78% in the prior session and up 3.38% over 20 sessions.
Playbook ✓

Bearish: underweight Japanese government bonds and avoid unhedged yen longs ahead of the vote. The trade is to short duration in JGBs or buy the yen-hedged equity leg only on a clear fiscal signal. Turn Bullish on the bond market if the government confirms fiscal discipline and the BOJ signals it will act against a disorderly rise in yields [[n3556]]. Turn more Bearish if the LDP’s mandate arrives with a spending plan that the bond market rejects. Japan is the one market where the vote hits rates, currency and equities at once.

geo.label: hiking into wage pressure
parts: Macro Stance

The RBA has hiked into a squeeze, and the economy is still overheating. The cash rate is at 3.85% after a 25 bps hike [[n0195]], and the RBA left the door open for more [[n0255]]. HSBC expects one more hike [[n0275]]. The WSJ says the overheating economy signals more rate pain ahead [[n0317]], and unions are pushing for above-inflation wage increases [[n0325]]. Real wages are not expected to grow until 2027 [[n0327]]. We stay Mixed: the rate cycle helps bank margins and hurts the households that borrow from them.
Demand & Financing

Households are paying for the hike. Major Australian banks raised home-loan rates after the decision [[n7215]], and the cost is a $1,300 blow for millions of mortgage holders [[n0196]]. The Australian dollar has been the offset: a higher dollar did not stop the RBA [[n0324]], and the AFR calls it a Hail Mary against inflation [[n0208]]. AUD/USD closed at 0.7023 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-04), up 4.24% over 20 sessions, and the S&P/ASX 200 closed at 8,927.80 AUD, up 2.45% over 20 sessions. The jobs market is feeling the squeeze too, with applications per role surging [[n0328]].
Playbook ✓

Mixed: favour the banks while margins are widening, and avoid housing-exposed names where rate pass-through is slowing demand. A higher Australian dollar also caps export-sector earnings, so keep it hedged. Turn Bullish on the broad market if the next inflation print confirms the RBA’s view and the hike stays a single move. Turn Bearish if wage data re-accelerate and the second hike that HSBC expects moves into the base case [[n0275]].

Use single-name exposure to KGHM only after its governance issues settle. Turn Bearish on the index if the rate pause turns into a reversal of the cutting path. ⚠ Divergence: the Warsaw index posted records [[n4314]] while the Polish IT sector is losing billions in value on the technology slump [[n4314]], so the index strength is coming from banks, energy and defence rather than from the technology names.
Narrative

The consensus is that AI capex keeps semiconductors and software on top. The New York Times added 450,000 digital subscribers [[n2245]], although its shares dropped despite a strong fourth quarter [[n2231]]. The Alphabet call highlights show the company’s spending plans in detail [[n2239]].

China’s strategic-inventory plans and the US stockpile are the demand, and the copper price fell anyway; copper is an asset here, not a gauge of China or global growth.
Narrative

The consensus is that real estate is a rates trade, and the driver that matters now is mortgage demand. The real estate ETF closed at 41.46, up 1.87% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-04). Rough winter weather hit homebuyers and tanked mortgage demand [[n7273]], and a surprising share of homeowners carry high mortgage rates [[n7270]].
Reported

The reported housing data are weak. A report says homeowners are falling behind on their mortgages [[n7171]], and mortgage demand is being hit by the weather [[n7273]]. Homebuilders are turning to the White House for help on an inventory glut [[n5811]] (with the Trump Homes plan under discussion [[n5809]]).
EPS Upside Watch

The homebuilders are set up for an upside surprise only if the government plan lands; the mortgage-rate constraint is still binding. The set-up favours the REITs with lower leverage and the mortgage-linked lenders that can benefit from a lower rate, but the default is a further mortgage drag.
⚡ Breaking Convention

The consensus is that a 1.87% rise over 20 sessions means the sector is stabilising, but the buyer-friendly headlines are coming from policy rather than demand. The breaking convention is that the sector is rising on a plan not yet in place, so treat the rally with caution.
Narrative

The consensus is that utilities are the defensive yield trade, and the driver that matters now is AI power demand. The utilities ETF closed at 43.08, up 0.40% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-04). The Tennessee Valley Authority is pursuing 6.2 gigawatts of new generation, citing data centres and population growth [[n6104]], and the AI boom is making natural gas great again [[n6106]].
Reported

Utilities are being asked to pay for the AI boom. Governor Shapiro is leaning on the tech industry to bear energy costs [[n6110]], and Musk’s plan to run data centres in space on solar power has experts doubtful [[n6115]]. The feed has no utility earnings headline in the window; the sector move is a power-demand move.
EPS Upside Watch

Utilities with generation and grid backlogs are set up for upside because the demand is contracted and the pricing is regulated. The TVA build-out supports the regional generators [[n6104]], and gas-fired generation benefits if the gas price holds. The merchant names carry the risk of a cap on power prices.
⚡ Breaking Convention

The consensus says utilities are bond proxies that fall when yields rise, but the 10-year is at 4.29% and the sector is still rising on power demand. The convention is breaking because growth in power demand is overriding rate sensitivity, so the market is paying for contracted capacity rather than for yield.
Narrative

The consensus is that European autos are a value and restructuring trade, and the driver that matters now is the defence of the sector by Brussels. The iShares STOXX Europe 600 Automobiles & Parts ETF closed at 47.26 EUR, up 4.94% over five sessions and down 0.16% over 20 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-04). Stellantis and Volkswagen are pressing the EU to defend the auto industry [[n6062]], and Ford and Geely are discussing a European production tie-up [[n6064]].
Reported

Volkswagen workers in Tennessee won a 20% pay rise in a union deal [[n6077]], and the UAW and Volkswagen reached a tentative deal at the Tennessee plant [[n6069]]. Stellantis faces Peugeot model delays from battery-plant snags [[n6085]], and an Italian watchdog blocked a BYD advert after a Stellantis complaint [[n6087]].
EPS Upside Watch

The set-up favours the makers with the fewest battery and plant delays and the most pricing power. Stellantis’ delays are the risk; Volkswagen’s labour deal is a cost headwind that is now priced. The Ford–Geely talks could be the upside for the European footprint if they progress.
⚡ Breaking Convention

The consensus says European autos are cheap and get a lift from political support, but the feed shows the support is coming through trade policy and advertising complaints rather than through demand. The convention is breaking: a BYD advert being blocked is the sign that the sector is defending a market, not growing one.
Narrative

The consensus is that US–Asia semiconductors are the core AI supply chain, and the driver that matters now is the chip-supply and demand split. The semiconductor ETF closed at 330.38, down 8.34% over five sessions and 4.42% in the prior session, but up 0.62% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-04). Nvidia AI chip sales to China have stalled under a US security review [[n5965]], and Cerebras, a rival to Nvidia, was valued at $23.1 billion in its latest financing [[n5980]].
Reported

AMD’s forecast shows tough competition in the AI trade [[n2246]] and its shares sank 17% [[n2244]]. Qualcomm’s forecast was hit by the memory shortage [[n2300]]. Micron fell 9.55% in the prior session after a rally [[n6027]] (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-04).
EPS Upside Watch

The set-up favours the memory and foundry names where supply, not demand, is the constraint. Qualcomm’s guidance shows the cost of that shortage [[n2300]]. Memory makers with pricing power are the upside case, but the chip designers face a pricing squeeze.
⚡ Breaking Convention

The consensus is that the memory shortage is a tailwind for memory makers, but Qualcomm’s guidance shows the shortage is a cost headwind for the device-chip designers [[n2300]]. The convention is breaking because scarcity is now a margin problem for the buyers, not a profit windfall for the sellers.

earnings_pattern.title: Earnings Pattern — Capex Gets Punished, Suppliers Get Paid
parts: Rewarded

The clearest reward went to the suppliers of the AI buildout. Broadcom and Nvidia shares rose on surging Google capital expenditure [[n5973]]. Super Micro raised its annual revenue forecast on strong server demand [[n2136]], which eased data-centre delay fears [[n2187]]. Snap rose on a fourth-quarter beat on sales [[n2243]], and E.l.f. Beauty beat and raised its full-year guidance [[n2223]]. Johnson Controls raised its FY26 guidance after a strong first quarter [[n2224]].
Punished

Results with cautious guidance or a capex surprise were punished. AMD’s stock sank 17% after its Q4 beat [[n2244]], the worst rout since 2018 [[n2273]]. Uber’s forecast fell below estimates and its shares dropped [[n2220]] [[n2219]]. Novo Nordisk sank 17% after a bleak 2026 forecast [[n2249]]. Boston Scientific beat, but its shares slid on a cautious 2026 revenue forecast [[n2236]]. AbbVie beat estimates and still fell [[n2214]].
Pattern

The pattern is that the spender is punished and the supplier rewarded. Alphabet’s spending plan spooked investors [[n5995]] even after a revenue beat [[n6002]] and a WSJ headline that Google is doubling spending [[n2210]]. The same week, the supply chain rose. A beat is not enough: the market prices guidance and capex, and a company that raises spending without a matching revenue line is treated as a cost, not an investment.
Attention into EPS

Into the next print the focus is on whether AI revenue catches up with AI capex. Amazon’s results come with a high bar, according to MarketWatch [[n2269]], and the next test is whether cloud growth justifies the spending plans. Super Micro’s raised outlook [[n2187]] is the other live test: the hardware names have to show that the backlog converts into revenue, not just that the demand exists.
Playbook

Own beats that come with a raised revenue outlook for the AI suppliers, and sell beats where the spender raises capex without a clear revenue line. Into the Amazon print, own the stock only with a defined stop, because the bar is high and the market punishes guidance that merely holds. Treat the suppliers as the cleaner exposure to the capex cycle, and the spenders as the trade that needs a revenue catalyst to work.

underowned.title: Japan’s bond curve: the fiscal rout that the BOJ says it will not stop
parts: Attention Gap

Most of the attention has gone to the yen and the election, but the bond market is the sharper signal. Reuters reports that the BOJ will not come to the rescue of a bond rout driven by Takaichi’s policies [[n3556]]. The Morningstar analysis of Japan’s bond selloff looks at the impact on banks and insurers [[n3554]], and the Japan Times warns that the bond market has a lesson for America [[n3563]]. The market’s attention is on the currency, and the rates story is less discussed than it should be.
Exposure & Risk

The instruments are JGB futures, the yen, and the Japanese banks and insurers that hold long-dated bonds. The risk is that a fiscal plan without a credible anchor pushes long-end yields higher and forces the BOJ to choose between the yen and the bond market. The feed’s Japanese bond-market analysis says the impact on equities is limited, but the impact on the insurers and the banks is the channel that matters [[n3554]].
Trigger to Watch

The theme becomes consensus when the government presents its fiscal plan after the vote and the BOJ signals action against a disorderly move in yields. Watch the long-end auction results and any BOJ comment on yields. Until then the bond curve is underowned because the election is pricing the currency, not the duration.

underowned.title: Venezuelan oil supply and the Gulf refiners: the barrels nobody is modelling
parts: Attention Gap

The oil debate is about Iran, but the supply story is Venezuela. A WSJ analysis says the $100 billion bet on Venezuelan oil relies on a broken state company [[n3261]], and Rystad says Venezuelan output will not top the region for years [[n3265]]. US refiners are struggling to absorb the sudden surge in Venezuelan imports [[n3202]], which is the physical bottleneck that the price headlines do not capture.
Exposure & Risk

The exposure is to the Gulf Coast refiners and to the oil majors with Venezuelan assets. The US is set to issue a general licence for oil production in Venezuela [[n3199]], and the US has sent $500 million of Venezuelan oil proceeds to Caracas [[n3270]]. Traders are rushing to lock in oil prices amid Iran risk and more Venezuelan supply [[n6030]]. The risk is that licence-driven supply arrives faster than refining capacity can absorb it, which would widen the spread between heavy and light crude.

The theme becomes consensus when the general licence is issued and the first large cargoes arrive at US refiners. Watch the refinery run rates and the spread on heavy crude. Venezuela’s government has said that oil prices will not be set by the US [[n6034]], so the pricing power is contested as well.

underowned.title: Critical-minerals price floors: the policy bid nobody is pricing in miners
parts: Attention Gap

The theme becomes consensus when the trade bloc sets out its price-floor terms or the US signs an offtake contract with a named miner. underowned.title: US natural gas: the AI power buildout is pulling gas back into the story

The theme becomes consensus when a utility or grid operator confirms new gas-fired capacity in its plan or a data-centre operator signs a long-dated gas supply contract. flows.title: Flows: liquidity is shifting from equities into the bond and dollar trade

Liquidity is tightening at the margins while the central banks argue about their own credibility. The global repo market is flagged as carrying risks in a $16 trillion government-backed market [[n2976]], and in Hong Kong the dollar slipped as loose liquidity revved up carry trades [[n2982]]. The 2-year closed at 3.57% and the 10-year at 4.29%, with a 10Y−2Y spread of 72 bps, up 1 bp over 20 observations (US Treasury, prior close 2026-02-04). The curve reads as steeper: investors are ramping up bets on a steeper curve under a Warsh-led Fed [[n8022]]. The dollar index closed at 97.62, up 1.21% over five sessions and down 0.97% over 20 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-04). Credit Check

Credit is where the stress is showing. The New York Times says private credit, once the hottest bet on Wall Street, has started to crack [[n6057]], and Bloomberg says AI’s lending risk is getting harder to compute [[n6060]]. Deutsche Bank is stuck with software loans [[n5737]]. A State Street private-credit ETF quintupled after a record inflow [[n5723]], which tells us the retail pipe is still open. Equity flows are rotating and the hedge-fund shorts are profiting. Hedge funds made $24 billion shorting software stocks so far in 2026, and they are increasing the bet [[n6020]]. Dip-buyers have gone missing as the software selloff slams stocks [[n6021]]. ETF demand surged in January, with record inflows to start 2026 [[n2962]]. The flow message is to lean defensive on duration and quality, and to avoid the software and private-credit beta. Keep duration near neutral until the jobs report and the Japanese bond auctions show whether the long end is breaking. Use the shorts-crowded software names as a tactical hedge rather than as a trade, because the hedge-fund short interest has already produced $24 billion of profit [[n6020]]. Keep EM exposure small until the Chinese and Japanese flows clarify.

anticipatory.title: US: February 11 payrolls and the Warsh confirmation
parts: What Is Priced

The market is pricing a soft jobs print and a Fed chair who may struggle to get his way. The January jobs report is set for February 11 after the shutdown delay [[n7230]], and ADP’s private payrolls missed expectations [[n7240]]. Warsh may struggle to get the votes he needs on the FOMC [[n8020]], and Senator Scott is facing a block on the nomination [[n8032]]. Investors are ramping up bets on a steeper curve under a Warsh-led Fed [[n8022]], and the Reuters poll expects rate-cut bets to cut the dollar rebound short [[n8025]].
Conditional Expression

If the payrolls print confirms the ADP shortfall, buy the front end and the duration hedge: the market will price a Fed that cuts to support jobs, and the dollar will fall. If the print beats and the Warsh confirmation stalls, sell the front end and keep the dollar, and avoid long-duration risk. Either way, keep a software hedge through the print, because the AI-disruption selloff is driving the equity move regardless of the labour data.
Risk

The risk is a Fed governance fight that outlasts the data. Trump’s Fed pick may surprise him [[n8017]], and Miran has quit the White House role to stay on at the Fed [[n8023]]. The risk is that a chair who cannot get votes steepens the curve for the wrong reasons, pushing the 10-year up on a credibility premium rather than on growth.

anticipatory.title: US–Iran talks and the oil risk premium
parts: What Is Priced

Oil is pricing a diplomatic path that is not yet agreed. US and Iranian nuclear talks are set for Oman [[n3255]], and the planned talks have revived de-escalation hopes [[n6031]]. Trump says Iran’s supreme leader should be very worried [[n6033]], and the US shot down an Iranian drone approaching an aircraft carrier [[n3254]]. Brent closed at 69.46 and WTI at 65.14, up 14.43% and 14.02% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-04).
Conditional Expression

If the Oman talks produce a framework, sell the energy rally and buy the broad market, because the risk premium is the first piece to go. If the talks break down or the drone incidents escalate, buy XLE and the integrated majors and add a gold hedge. The asymmetry is that a headline de-escalation can remove the premium in a single session, so keep the energy position sized for a fast reversal.
Risk

The risk is an incident at sea or in the air that turns the talks into a strike. The US is shooting down drones near the carrier group [[n3254]], and the Iranian supreme leader’s rhetoric is hardening [[n6033]]. A strike would overwhelm the diplomatic discount and push oil well above its current level.

anticipatory.title: Ukraine: the first productive day of US-backed talks
parts: What Is Priced

Ukraine talks are the pending event. Ukraine and Russia wrapped a productive first day of US-backed peace talks [[n3247]], with the trilateral talks resuming in the UAE after a major energy attack [[n3249]]. The Guardian asks how close a peace deal is and what each side wants [[n3246]]. The market is pricing a path to a ceasefire, which would hit defence and the energy-security premium.
Conditional Expression

If the talks produce a durable ceasefire, buy the European cyclicals and the utilities with Ukrainian reconstruction exposure, and sell the defence names that had the security premium. If the talks stall and the energy attacks continue, buy the defence and the Polish defence names, and keep the energy-security trade in place. The asymmetry is that a ceasefire removes the defence premium quickly, while a stall rebuilds it more slowly.
Risk

The risk is that talks are reported as productive while the strikes continue. The NYT reports the talks resumed after a huge attack by Moscow [[n3245]], so the market will read every headline. A ceasefire that is announced and then violated would hit credibility and leave the defence trade stranded.

anticipatory.title: Japan’s election and the fiscal mandate
parts: What Is Priced

The market is pricing a strong mandate and a fiscal plan that the bond market has not yet accepted. The BOJ will not come to the rescue of the Takaichi-driven bond rout [[n3556]], and the dollar firmed and the yen came under pressure ahead of the elections [[n8112]]. Analysts are asking why Japan’s election matters for the world [[n3570]], and Takaichi is seen avoiding a plan to cut Lower House seats [[n3581]].
Conditional Expression

If the LDP wins a clear mandate with a credible fiscal anchor, buy the Japanese equities on a hedged basis and sell long-end JGBs into any rally. If the mandate arrives with a spending plan the bond market rejects, short the yen and the long end, and buy the Nikkei only through a currency hedge. The vote is a fiscal event as much as a political one.
Risk

The risk is a bond-market revolt that forces the BOJ into a choice. A bond rout that the BOJ refuses to stop would push yields up across the curve and hit the banks and insurers that hold the paper [[n3554]]. The yen weakness, if it continues, is what brings intervention back into the story.

catalysts.title: $GOOGL — capex shock, revenue beat

The catalyst is Alphabet’s fourth-quarter print: the company beat on revenue and projected a significant increase in AI spending [[n6002]], and Reuters says its 2026 capital spending could double while the cloud business booms [[n5993]]. The hurdle is that the stock must recover the post-print drop, which CNBC described as capex plans spooking investors [[n5995]]. The risk is that the spending outruns the cloud revenue and the margin compresses.
Trade Expression

Hold the stock at a neutral weight with a defined stop, rather than adding into the print reaction. A pair against a software name exposed to the same AI-disruption theme is a cleaner expression. The trade is invalidated if cloud growth is confirmed and the capex is matched by a revenue line, or if the software selloff spreads to search and ads.

catalysts.title: $AMD — the worst rout since 2018

Short AMD into strength rather than into the low, sized small given the size of the move. The trade is invalidated if the company raises guidance or if a credible accelerator order from a hyperscaler is confirmed, which would show the competitive fear is overdone.

catalysts.title: $NVDA — the buyer of the sell-off

The catalyst is the rally in Nvidia and Broadcom on surging Google capital expenditure [[n5973]], and the chief executive’s call that the software selloff is the most illogical thing in the world [[n5972]]. Buy on weakness with a stop below the five-session low, sized for a volatile tape. The trade is invalidated if the China sale remains stalled [[n5965]] for another quarter, or if a hyperscaler cuts its capex plan, which would break the supplier thesis.

catalysts.title: $NVO — a bleak 2026 forecast

Its chief executive warned it will get worse before it gets better [[n8068]]. The thesis is that pricing, not volume, is the problem, and the reset is not finished.

The feed does not carry a Novo Nordisk price in the market card, so no price is quoted. The hurdle is that the reset may already be priced; the risk is that the company’s guidance is revised again, or that the US pricing rules spread to launches in Europe [[n6164]].

Underweight the stock into any bounce until the pricing terms are clear, or express it through a relative trade against the obesity peer. The trade is invalidated if the company reaffirms guidance with a credible pricing plan.

catalysts.title: $ORCL — the OpenAI dependency
parts: Catalyst & Thesis

The catalyst is the WSJ analysis of what Oracle has to lose from the OpenAI and Nvidia relationship turning rocky [[n5978]]. Short or put-spread Oracle into bounces rather than into the low, with the stop above the five-session high. The trade is invalidated if OpenAI funding is confirmed with a long-dated Oracle contract, which would remove the concentration concern.

catalysts.title: $SMCI — the raised outlook
parts: Catalyst & Thesis

The catalyst is Super Micro’s raised annual revenue forecast on strong server demand [[n2136]], which Bloomberg says eased data-centre delay fears [[n2187]]. The thesis is that the server maker is converting the AI backlog into revenue, and the raised guidance is the proof.
Price Hurdle & Risk

The feed does not carry a Super Micro price in the market card, so no price is quoted. The hurdle is that the raised outlook may already be in the price after the prior session’s supplier rally. The risk is that the data-centre delays return and the revenue timing slips.

Buy on a pullback below the post-guidance level with a stop under the outlook. The trade is invalidated if the company cuts its revenue guidance or if its customers push out data-centre builds.

retail_intro: Figma’s sell-off has become an explicit retail bargain debate, while disappointing chip forecasts and weight-loss pricing pressure test the idea that a strong product guarantees a good stock.

retail.title: Figma / FIG — cheaper shares need a valuation case
parts: Why Retail Is Here

Figma supplies the familiar emotional contrast between a product people recognise and a share price they dislike. Stocktwits reports that the stock has fallen more than 40% this year and that retail traders regard it as a steal. [[n4530]] That is direct evidence of the bargain narrative, rather than enthusiasm inferred from an unrelated technology stock. The attractive interpretation is that a large decline has made a promising business accessible. The dangerous interpretation is that the size of the fall itself proves the future return. An investor can be correct that a product is valuable while paying too much for the earnings the shareholder will eventually receive.
What Is Driving It

The dated catalyst is the continuing drawdown and the retail response to it, not a new reported earnings beat. Stocktwits' headline defines both the decline and the optimistic interpretation. [[n4530]] The useful question is what must be true about future demand, pricing and costs for the new entry price to work. A share that has fallen sharply may require less perfection than before, yet still leave little room for slower growth or heavier competition. Separate the proposition that the market's expectations have reset from the proposition that those expectations are now too low. The first follows from a large repricing; the second needs a business and valuation argument.
The Social Signal

The phrase 'a steal now' makes the psychology unusually clear. [[n4530]] The buyer is invited to measure the opportunity against an earlier quote, so the old price becomes an anchor even when it was never a reliable estimate of value. That can produce patient ownership if the business delivers, or repeated averaging down if every lower quote is treated as a better bargain by definition. The source describes a retail interpretation; it does not establish a market-wide survey or a ranking of the most-owned shares. Treat the discussion as evidence of the argument being made and look for operating facts that could eventually settle it.
Historical Analog

The mechanical analogy is the post-listing growth-stock reset. Early enthusiasm establishes an ambitious reference price; a later decline brings a second wave of buyers who feel they are obtaining the original opportunity at a discount. That second wave may be buying genuine improvement in expected return, but it can also be buying the memory of an expensive first wave. The relevant lesson is about anchoring, not a prediction that every technology listing follows the same path. A percentage decline has no natural stopping point when the earnings base is still being debated. The investor needs a reason why the business should justify the current quote, rather than a reason why it once traded higher.
Smart Money View

A constructive professional can share the interest in the product while insisting on a margin of safety in the operating assumptions. Examine whether customer demand can turn into cash after the spending required to retain and expand those relationships. The cautious view asks what competition can do to pricing and what growth the valuation already requires. Neither side can be settled by the retail headline alone. Use an equity position sized for uncertainty rather than a leveraged attempt to capture the exact bottom. A gradual entry preserves the ability to respond when business evidence becomes clearer; an all-in recovery trade makes patience depend on the next price move.
When the Narrative Breaks

The narrative breaks if the main reason for each additional purchase remains that the shares are lower than the first purchase. Set a limit on the capital committed before adding. Reassess when company evidence changes the expected demand or cash-generation path, and reduce if the valuation still needs an implausibly favourable outcome. A constructive signal would be operating progress that makes the investment case stronger independently of the share's previous high. A weakening signal would be a succession of attractive explanations that leaves the economic forecast unchanged. The task is to buy an adequately priced business, not to prove that the original sell-off went too far.

Where It Breaks

Own the share only with a demand and competitive-position thesis that can survive an ordinary outcome. The narrative weakens if the response to each forecast disappointment is simply that AI must eventually reward every supplier. Where It Breaks
